core: Apply the action directly onto a thing
hint: Takes a verb that wanders and points it at an object — covering it, treating it, doing it all over.
feeling: be- is a hand pressing down on a surface. It takes an intransitive verb — one that just happens — and forces it to land on a direct object. Sprechen is to speak, floating; besprechen is to speak all over a topic until it is covered. Wherever you meet be-, expect the accusative: no über, no zu, no preposition at all. The thing itself becomes the target. Native speakers feel it as thoroughness plus contact — the action is not just aimed at something, it is spread onto it.
mnemonic: Rule of thumb: be- = 'do X to it, all over it'. If a preposition disappears, be- ate it.

examples.why: Answering used to need auf. be- swallows the preposition — you now answer the question itself.
Speech spread over a topic until every part is covered, rather than speech drifting outward.
Climbing stops being 'going up' and becomes an act performed on a mountain.
Paint applied over a surface. Malen makes a picture; bemalen covers an object.
Your step lands on a specific floor. The room becomes what you do the stepping to.
Wohnen in is living somewhere; bewohnen makes the house the thing you occupy.
Writing spread across a subject until its shape is visible — writing onto a thing.
Work applied to a specific object until it changes. Not labour in general — labour on this.
The coming lands on you. Something arrives at your surface, so you end up holding it.
Zahlen is to pay in general; bezahlen settles a specific bill — payment applied to a thing.

core: Away from, off, out of — separation and release
hint: The un- prefix: removing, escaping, or emerging out of something.
feeling: ent- is the moment two things come apart. Sometimes it removes (entdecken — take the cover off), sometimes it escapes (entlaufen — run away from), sometimes it is the reverse gear of a verb (entspannen — un-tension). There is a second, quieter branch: emergence, coming out of a source (entstehen — to arise). Both branches share one gesture — a boundary being crossed outward. If English would reach for un-, de-, or -away, German usually reaches for ent-.
mnemonic: Feel it as a snap apart. Note it often takes a dative of the thing escaped from: dem Feuer entkommen.

examples.why: Running plus a boundary: you leave the person or place you belonged to. Takes the dative.
Decken is to cover. Remove the cover and the thing underneath appears — literally un-cover.
Letting go plus separation: the person is let loose from the institution holding them.
Spannen is to stretch tight. ent- releases the tension — the string goes slack.
Fleeing already means running; ent- adds the thing you break away from, in the dative.
The emergence branch: something steps out of nothing and stands there. Origin, not removal.
Scheiden is to separate. You pull the options apart and cut one loose from the rest.
Guilt (Schuld) is removed from the person. ent- lifts it off like a coat.
Leading plus away: you lead someone out of where they belong. Same logic as entlaufen, but done to them.
Bureaucratic humour: the Sorge (worry) is removed. The rubbish, and your problem, go away.

core: A sound-variant of ent- — receiving, sensing, rising toward
hint: A tiny closed set: only three real verbs exist. Learn them, don't try to build more.
feeling: emp- is not a productive prefix — it is ent- that softened before f for ease of pronunciation, and it froze that way in exactly three verbs: empfangen, empfehlen, empfinden. The feeling that survives is ent-'s outward movement turned inward: something comes toward you and you take it in. Reception rather than removal. Be honest with yourself about this one — you recognise emp-, you never generate it. The list below gives the three verbs plus their everyday derivatives, which is the whole family.
mnemonic: Three roots only: -fangen (catch), -fehlen (commend), -finden (sense). Everything else is a derivative.

examples.why: Fangen is to catch. You catch what comes toward you — a guest, a signal, a parcel.
Old sense: to commend something into someone's care — you hand it toward them.
Finding turned inward: you find something inside yourself rather than out in the world.
Someone who senses too much and too easily — the feeling arrives and lands hard.
The gentler adjective: inclined to feel deeply. Same inward-sensing root.
The place or moment where things are caught as they arrive — hotel desk, party, signal.
The one doing the catching, in a letter or on a radio.
The thing you hand toward someone as worth having.
The noun of inward finding: what you notice inside yourself.
Compound of the catching sense — a device or a host open to what is coming.

core: Carry the action through to its result
hint: The action reaches completion — achievement, or death.
feeling: er- is an arrow finally hitting the target. It takes a verb of process and adds the endpoint: not doing, but having got there. Arbeiten is to work; erarbeiten is to work until you own the result. That endpoint can be a triumph (erreichen, erfinden) or a death (erschießen, ertrinken) — German uses the same gesture for both, because both are the action pushed all the way to where it stops. There is also a birth branch: erwachen, erblühen, something coming into being. Emergence and completion are the same arc seen from either end.
mnemonic: Ask: 'and then what happened?' er- is the answer. Effort → outcome, or process → finality.

examples.why: Reichen is to extend toward. er- lands it: your hand actually arrives at the thing.
Finding pushed past discovery: you keep going until the thing you found didn't exist before.
Knowing arrives in one moment — the point at which acquaintance snaps into identification.
Waiting with its endpoint attached: you wait for a result you already picture.
Counting things out one after another until the whole sequence is delivered.
Lernen is studying; erlernen is studying until the skill is fully acquired and yours.
Shooting carried to its final result. The clearest case of er- as 'all the way to the end'.
Grim logic: you take in water until the process completes. The endpoint is fatal.
Freezing pushed past discomfort to its absolute conclusion.
The emergence branch: consciousness comes into being. Same arc, arriving at a beginning.

core: Gathered, brought to a whole — mostly fossilised
hint: Ancient 'together / completed'. In modern German it's frozen: recognise it, don't build with it.
feeling: ge- once meant together and brought to completion — you can still see it alive in nouns (Gebirge, a whole range of mountains; Gespräch, speech gathered into a conversation) and in the past participle itself (ge-macht — the doing, completed). As a verb prefix it has gone fossil: the meanings drifted centuries ago and no longer decompose cleanly. Treat this list as a set to memorise rather than a pattern to apply — but the faint scent of 'brought fully together' is still there in most of them if you look.
mnemonic: Learn these as vocabulary. The one living use of ge- is the past participle: ge-sag-t, ge-lauf-en.

examples.why: Old sense: to be within earshot of, therefore under someone's authority. Takes the dative.
It 'falls together' well with you — it suits. Note the reversal: es gefällt mir.
The parts come together properly. Also dative: es ist mir gelungen.
Old winnan = to strive. ge- brings the striving to its completed, successful whole.
To stand fully behind something — the whole truth brought out and stood on.
Related to 'to use, take'. ge- makes it total: taking something in fully.
Brauchen is to need; ge- turns need into completed application — putting it to use.
You land somewhere without steering — the outcome comes together around you.
Thinking gathered and formalised into remembrance. Takes the genitive.
Horchen is to listen closely. ge- completes it: listening that ends in doing.

core: Wrong, failed, badly done
hint: The exact twin of English mis-. Clean, transparent, easy to trust.
feeling: miss- is the easiest prefix in German because it means what your ear already expects: something has gone wrong, been done badly, or failed outright. It maps onto English mis- almost perfectly (missverstehen / misunderstand). The feeling is a judgement — not just a description of an action but a verdict on it. Two small mechanics: it is unstressed and inseparable, and in the perfect tense it takes no ge- (ich habe es missverstanden).
mnemonic: If English would say mis-, German almost certainly says miss-. Trust the cognate.

examples.why: Understanding that went the wrong way. The verdict prefix sits on top of the action.
The direct opposite of gelingen: the parts did not come together. Dative: es misslang mir.
Use bent in the wrong direction — the thing was used, but wrongly.
Trust judged as misplaced. Takes the dative: ich misstraue ihm.
Exact mirror of gefallen: it falls together badly with you.
Attention (achten) given wrongly — that is, not given at all.
Glücken is to turn out lucky. miss- flips the luck.
Interpretation that points at the wrong thing.
Geraten is to end up somewhere; miss- makes that somewhere the wrong place.
Handling done badly — the verdict applied to physical treatment of a person.

core: Four feelings: away, wrong, transformed, used up
hint: The biggest and most slippery prefix. Learn its four branches and most of it resolves.
feeling: ver- is really three old prefixes that collapsed into one, which is why it feels chaotic. It has four branches. (1) Away / gone — verkaufen, verschwinden: the thing leaves. (2) Wrong, almost always reflexive — sich verlaufen, sich versprechen: the action misfired. (3) Transformation — verbessern, sich verlieben: something becomes a new state. (4) Used up / to exhaustion — verbrauchen, verschlafen: the action consumes its object or its time. When you meet a new ver- verb, run those four in order; one of them almost always fits.
mnemonic: Reflexive sich ver- = 'I did it wrong'. That single rule unlocks a whole class: versprechen, verlaufen, verwählen, verschreiben.

examples.why: Branch 1, away: buying with the direction reversed — the goods leave your hands.
Schwinden is to dwindle. ver- takes the dwindling all the way to gone.
Branch 2, wrong: your walking went astray. Reflexive marks the error as yours.
Same reflexive logic. Note the non-reflexive versprechen = to promise: words given away.
Branch 3, transformation: ver- moves the thing into a better state.
Transformation of a person: you don't do loving, you become someone in love.
Branch 4: needing carried until nothing is left. The fuel is gone.
Sleeping that consumes the time it should have fit inside. You slept the morning away.
The old root means 'to grasp'. ver- takes the grasp away — the memory slips out of hold.
Bieten is to offer. ver- turns the offer against itself: the thing is offered away from you.

core: Into pieces — destruction and dispersal
hint: The most physical prefix in German. Something whole becomes fragments.
feeling: zer- is a single, unambiguous image: a thing coming apart into pieces. Unlike ver-, it has no second branch and no figurative drift to speak of — whatever verb you attach it to, the object ends up fragmented, scattered, or ruined. That reliability makes it a good prefix to learn early, because it also teaches you the shape of the system: attach the gesture to any action verb and you can predict the meaning without a dictionary. If you can break it, you can zer- it.
mnemonic: Picture a plate hitting the floor. Every zer- verb is that image applied to a different action.

examples.why: Breaking, but into many pieces rather than two. zer- multiplies the fracture.
Stören is to disturb. zer- pushes disturbance to total ruin.
Tearing that doesn't stop at one rip — the paper ends up in fragments.
Cutting applied until the thing is no longer one thing.
Laying out the parts separately — controlled fragmentation, as with an engine or an argument.
Falling apart from the inside. Empires and buildings both zerfallen.
Pressing until the structure gives way — potatoes, or a cigarette.

examples.english: to chop up, reduce in size
examples.why: Deliberately making something into small pieces. The cooking-verb version of zer-.
Wood, glass, or a political party — all break into shards the same way.
Bursting where the pieces fly outward, not just a pop.

core: Off, away, down — detachment from a starting point
hint: Something leaves a surface, a place, or a list. The counterpart of an-.
feeling: ab- is a hand pulling something off. The core image is detachment: a train leaving a platform, a hat coming off a head, a task coming off a list. It carries a faint sense of subtraction — abnehmen is both 'take off' and 'lose weight', because both are removal from a total. A second use is downward motion (absteigen), and a third is completion-by-removal: once the thing is off, the job is done (abschließen). Where an- attaches, ab- detaches — learning them as a pair is the fastest route in.
mnemonic: Think of a sticker being peeled. If English says off, de-, or -away, German often says ab-.

examples.why: The vehicle detaches from the station. Motion plus separation from a starting point.

examples.english: to take off; to lose weight
examples.why: Taking something off a surface — or off your body. Removal from a total in both senses.
Cutting with the result that a piece separates. The bread and the slice part ways.
Saying something off the calendar — the event is detached from the plan.
Fetching plus removal: you take the person or parcel away from where it was waiting.
Closing so completely that it's sealed off. Same word for a door and a degree.

examples.english: to switch off; to put down
examples.why: Putting a thing down and away from you — the appliance is detached from its power.

examples.english: to wash off, do the dishes
examples.why: Washing with the goal of removing what's stuck on. The dirt comes off.
Both: taking a picture off a hook, and (with von) hanging off something else.
Breaking that ends the connection — a branch, or a conversation you stop mid-way.

core: Toward and touching — contact, attachment, switching on
hint: The action reaches a target and makes contact. Also the moment something starts.
feeling: an- is the click of two things touching. It takes an action and gives it a target it actually reaches: rufen is to shout into the air; anrufen is to shout at a specific person, which is why it means to phone them. From contact come two extensions: switching on (anmachen — the current makes contact) and beginning (anfangen — the action makes first contact with the world). Emotionally, an- can be a bit confrontational — anschreien is not shouting near someone but shouting at them. Contact always has a direction.
mnemonic: an- = the arrow reaches and touches. Its opposites are ab- (off) and aus- (out/off).

examples.why: Calling aimed at one person until it connects. Contact made — hence a phone call.
The moment the action first catches hold. First contact between you and the task.

examples.english: to switch on; to hit on sb
examples.why: Making contact with the circuit. The flirting sense is the same idea, applied to a person.
Coming until you touch the destination. The journey meets its endpoint.
Pulling clothes onto the body, or pulling something toward you. Both close a distance.
Seeing pointed at a specific target — your gaze lands on it rather than wandering.
The offer is extended toward a person until it reaches them. Takes the dative.
Holding applied to motion — you bring the movement into contact with a standstill.
The most literal case: grasping that actually makes contact with the surface.
Screaming aimed at a person. The difference between shouting and shouting at is just an-.

core: Up, open, onto — rising and unsealing
hint: Upward motion, opening something closed, or landing onto a surface.
feeling: auf- has two gestures that feel like one: up (aufstehen, aufheben) and open (aufmachen, aufblühen) — because to open something is usually to lift its lid. Underneath both sits the preposition's own meaning, on top of, which gives a third use: applying something onto a surface (aufschreiben — writing onto paper). There's also a sudden-onset flavour, the moment something springs up: aufwachen, aufschrecken. The odd one out is aufhören (to stop) — treat it as an exception and move on.
mnemonic: Lid lifting. auf- = up / open / onto. Its natural opposites are zu- (shut) and ab- (down, off).

examples.why: The purest case: standing plus upward. Out of bed, or up from a chair.
Making something open — the lid, the door, the shop. The 'open' gesture in its plainest form.
Consciousness springing up. The sudden-onset flavour of auf-.
Lifting up off the ground — and by extension keeping it, since you didn't put it back.
Confusing for English speakers: German sees writing onto a surface, not down.
Building upward from nothing — a tent, a company, an argument.
A flower opening. Used of people too: someone who opens up and comes alive.
Clearing with an upward, restorative sense: things get lifted back into their places.
Handing the thing up and out of your hands — you release it to someone or something else.
The exception. No transparent logic survives — memorise it as a fixed pair.

core: Out, out of, and out to the very end
hint: Motion outward, switching off, or doing something exhaustively until nothing is left.
feeling: aus- starts as pure geometry — out of a container (aussteigen, auspacken). Two extensions follow naturally. First, switching off: ausmachen, because the light goes out. Second, and more interesting for a learner, exhaustiveness: if you do something aus-, you do it until the supply runs out. Austrinken is not to drink but to finish the glass; ausschlafen is to sleep until you have no sleep left. That second branch is where aus- gets genuinely useful — it turns an activity into a completed one.
mnemonic: Empty the container. Either something comes out of it, or you keep going until it's empty.

examples.why: Leaving the house — and also 'to run out', as in supplies. Out of a space, out of a stock.
The light goes out. Direct opposite of anmachen: contact broken instead of made.
Climbing out of a vehicle. Also figurative: to quit a project or a lifestyle.

examples.english: to take off; to move out
examples.why: Pulling clothes off the body, or pulling yourself out of a flat. Same outward tug.
Pressing until the content comes out — a lemon, or a thought.
Exhaustive branch: drinking until the glass is empty. Not the act, the completion.
Sleeping until you've used up all the sleep you needed. A very German concept.
Filling every field until none is left blank — filling to exhaustion, not outward.

examples.english: to unpack; to spill the beans
examples.why: Taking things out of a box — or taking the truth out of yourself.
Choosing one thing out of a set. The chosen item leaves the group.

core: Alongside, added to, present with
hint: A small, slightly formal set: something is placed next to or added into something else.
feeling: bei- is the preposition bei (at, near, alongside) doing prefix duty. The gesture is placing one thing beside another so it joins it — an enclosure in a letter, a person standing next to you in a crisis, a member added to a club. It is a low-frequency prefix and it leans formal or written; you will meet it far more in a contract or a newspaper than in conversation. Almost every bei- verb takes a dative, because the whole idea is proximity to something.
mnemonic: Placing a card next to the pile. Expect the dative: er trug der Diskussion bei.

examples.why: Carrying your piece over and setting it beside the shared pile. Dative + zu.
Bringing knowledge alongside a person until they have it. Dative for the learner.
Laying a document beside the main one inside the envelope. The literal core.
Standing next to someone in difficulty. Physical position as emotional loyalty.
Stepping into position alongside the existing members. Dative: dem Verein beitreten.
Formal: to be located alongside an event as it happens.
Adding one substance alongside another in a mixture.
Bureaucratic cousin of beilegen — joining a thing onto the end of a document.
Keeping something alongside you as things change — a habit, a policy, a name.
Formal funeral verb: setting the person beside those already there.

core: Into, inward — entering and settling
hint: Something moves in and stays there. The prefix form of the preposition in.
feeling: ein- is a thing going into a container and staying. The literal cases are easy (einsteigen, einpacken, einatmen), but the useful ones are where the container is abstract: einschlafen is sinking into sleep, einsehen is seeing into a matter until you accept it, einführen is leading something into a country or a conversation. Watch for the settling nuance too — sich einleben, einziehen: not just entering but coming to rest inside. Note that ein- as a prefix has nothing to do with ein meaning 'one'.
mnemonic: Arrow pointing into a box. Opposite: aus-. Pair them (einsteigen / aussteigen) and both stick.

examples.why: Climbing into a vehicle. The exact mirror of aussteigen.
Loading someone into your event or home. The same verb loads a truck.
Buying things into the household. The goods come inside; hence groceries.
Sinking into sleep. Not the state, the entry into it — which is why it's a different verb.
Breathing inward. Its opposite, ausatmen, shows the pair working perfectly.
Leading something in — a product into a market, a topic into a talk, a person into a role.
Putting things into the bag. Opposite of auspacken.
Pulling yourself into a new home. The settling nuance: you arrive and stay.
Setting something into position so it starts working — a part, a team, a rule.
Seeing into a matter deeply enough to concede it. Ich sehe das ein = fair enough, I get it.

core: Away — and, by extension, onward
hint: Departure, plus the sense of carrying on. Slightly literary next to weg-.
feeling: fort- means away, and it overlaps heavily with weg-: fortgehen and weggehen are near-twins, with fort- the more written, slightly older-sounding option. Its distinctive second sense is the one worth learning: onward continuation. If something goes away from you along a line, it keeps going — hence fortsetzen (continue), fortschreiten (progress), Fortschritt (progress, the noun). Same gesture, two readings: leaving, or carrying on. Context tells you which, and usually the verb is fixed in one sense anyway.
mnemonic: 'Away along a line.' If it's about leaving, weg- is more natural in speech; fort- for continuation.

examples.why: The plain departure sense. Slightly more formal than weggehen.
The continuation branch: you set the thing further along its line.
Both readings in one verb — carry on speaking, or drive away. Context decides.

examples.english: to run away; to run on
examples.why: Same duality: a child running off, or a number series running onward.
Existence carried onward past the point it might have stopped.
Striding onward. The source of Fortschritt — progress as steps taken forward.
Educating yourself onward past your current level. Common in job listings.
Moving a thing away from where it is. The neutral, technical use.
Pulling yourself away from a town for good. Stronger than umziehen.
Hunting someone away from the place — the aggressive end of the departure sense.

core: Toward the speaker — 'this way, come here'
hint: Direction relative to you. The mirror of hin-. Master the pair and dozens of compounds open up.
feeling: her- means toward me, the speaker. It carries no meaning of its own beyond direction, which is exactly why it is powerful: German encodes viewpoint into the verb, where English uses tone or context. Komm her! is come here. Its real value is in compounds with other prepositions: herein (in, toward me), herunter (down, toward me), heraus (out, toward me). In spoken German these shorten — reinkommen, runterkommen. If you learn nothing else about direction prefixes, learn that her = here, hin = there.
mnemonic: her ≈ here. The vowels even match. Compounds: her + ein/aus/unter/über/auf.

examples.why: Coming in the direction of the speaker. Wo kommst du her? = where are you from?
Carrying something toward me. Hinbringen would carry it away to somewhere else.
Giving in my direction. There's often a note of reluctance — hand it over.
Placing something 'here' into existence — the factory brings it into our world.
Going to get something and bringing it back to where I am.
Managing to get something to arrive at you. Often Wo bekomme ich das her?
Running toward the speaker. Also hinter jdm herlaufen — to run after someone.
Wo nimmst du das her? — where are you taking that from, to bring it here?
Extending your arm so the thing comes to my side.
Figurative: the cause moves toward the present from somewhere back there.

core: Away from the speaker, toward a target — 'that way'
hint: The mirror of her-. Motion out from you toward a destination.
feeling: hin- is the outbound arrow: away from me, toward there. It answers wohin? — where to. Where her- pulls things toward the speaker, hin- sends them out: hingehen (go there), hinlegen (lay it down over there), hinsehen (look over that way). Like her-, it stacks with prepositions to make precise compounds — hinauf, hinunter, hinaus, hinein. There's also a downward flavour in some verbs (hinfallen — to fall over), because falling is motion away from your upright self toward the ground.
mnemonic: hin = thither, her = hither. Ich gehe hin (I go there) / Komm her (come here).

examples.why: Walking toward a destination away from the current position. Answers wohin?
Same arrow, by vehicle. Fährst du hin? — are you going there?
Placing something down over there. Reflexively, sich hinlegen = to lie down.
Putting yourself down into a spot. The hin supplies the target position.
Standing an object in a particular place away from you.
Directing your gaze outward to a point. Schau mal hin!
Falling away from your upright position toward the ground. The downward flavour.
Carrying something away to a destination. Exact opposite of herbringen.
Pointing away from yourself at the thing you want noticed. Takes auf + accusative.
Sending your attention outward toward a sound instead of just hearing it.

core: Released, broken free — and therefore off we go
hint: Something is let loose. Either it starts suddenly, or you get rid of it.
feeling: los- comes from the adjective los (loose, free) and it does two related jobs. First, release: loslassen — let go, losbinden — untie, loswerden — get rid of. Second, and more common in daily speech, sudden starting: once a thing is released it moves, so losfahren is to set off, losgehen is for something to kick off, loslegen is to get stuck in. That energetic, informal quality is the giveaway — los- verbs sound like the starting pistol. Los! on its own means 'go!'.
mnemonic: The dog off the leash. Release → motion → 'and off we go'.

examples.why: The vehicle is released from standstill. The most common start-sense los- verb.
Wann geht's los? — when does it start? The event is let loose.
The purest case: your grip opens and the thing is free.
Becoming free of something. Takes an accusative object: ich werde ihn nicht los.
Undoing the knot so the thing is loose. Release in its literal, physical form.
Colloquial and energetic: to start with real momentum. Leg los!
Running released from stillness — the sprint start.
Turning until the part comes free. Release applied to fastenings.
Freeing yourself from a group, an idea, or a dependency.
A storm or an argument bursting loose all at once. Sudden onset at full force.

core: Together with, joining in — participation
hint: Someone or something does the action alongside the others. The friendliest prefix.
feeling: mit- is the one your friends described, and it is the cleanest example of the whole system: whatever verb follows, someone is doing it together with someone else. Kommen is to come; mitkommen is to come along with us. It never means anything else. Two nuances worth noticing. First, the 'with whom' is often left unsaid because the prefix already implies the group — Kommst du mit? needs no object. Second, it can carry a warm, inclusive tone: mitdenken, mitfühlen, mitmachen all describe someone showing up for the shared effort.
mnemonic: Always 'along with us'. If a person or thing is included in the action, mit- is the prefix.

examples.why: Coming as part of the group. Kommst du mit? — the object is understood.
Doing the thing alongside everyone else rather than watching.
Taking a thing or person with you when you go. Also: zum Mitnehmen = takeaway.
Bringing something with you to where you're going — wine, a friend, bad news.
Teilen is to share. Sharing information with someone. Takes the dative.
Travelling in someone else's vehicle. Source of Mitfahrgelegenheit — a lift.

examples.english: to play along, join the game
examples.why: Being included in the game — or, figuratively, going along with a plan.
Working as part of a shared effort. Mitarbeiter = colleague, co-worker.
Praise in German workplaces: thinking with the team rather than just following orders.
Joining your voice to the others. The most literal 'together' there is.

core: After, behind, in pursuit — and doing it again to check
hint: The action follows something else in time or space: chasing, copying, or verifying.
feeling: nach- means after, and everything grows from that. Physically it is pursuit: nachlaufen, running after. In time it is doing something later or a second time — which becomes the very useful checking sense: nachschauen, nachfragen, nachschlagen all mean going back over something to verify it. A third branch is imitation, following someone's model: nachmachen, nachahmen. And a fourth, softer one: yielding, letting the other person go first — nachgeben, nachlassen. All four are the same posture: you are behind, and the other thing leads.
mnemonic: You are in second position. Chasing it, copying it, checking it, or giving way to it.

examples.why: Thinking that comes after the event — going back over it in your head. Takes über.
Looking again, after the fact, to make sure. Everyday verifying sense.

examples.english: to look up in a book
examples.why: Literally striking the pages open after the question arose. Dictionary verb.
Asking a follow-up — a question that comes after the first answer.
Doing what someone did, afterwards. Following their model step for step.
The more formal cousin. Same idea: your action trails theirs.
The literal core. Also figurative: chasing after someone's approval. Dative.
Giving ground and moving into the position behind. Conceding the lead.
The pain or the storm lets up — it falls behind its previous intensity.

examples.english: to catch up on, make up for
examples.why: Fetching what you missed and bringing it into the present. Sleep, work, a birthday.

core: Down, downward, laid low
hint: Literary and formal. Downward motion, often with force or ceremony.
feeling: nieder- means down, and it is the higher-register alternative to hinunter- or ab-. You meet it in three settings: physical lowering with some weight to it (niederlegen, niederknien), forceful suppression (niederschlagen, niederreißen), and formal or written registers (niederschreiben — to set down in writing). It rarely appears in casual speech, so treat it as a reading prefix: you want to recognise it in news, history, and literature rather than deploy it at the bakery. The related adjective is niedrig — low.
mnemonic: 'Down, with weight or ceremony.' If plain 'down' will do, spoken German picks runter-.

examples.why: Laying something down formally — flowers, weapons, or an office you hold.
Striking downward. Used of people and of uprisings alike.
Writing down, in the formal register. Records and testimony rather than shopping lists.
Burning until the structure is down. The endpoint is total.
Lowering yourself onto your knees. Ceremonial and physical at once.
Pulling a structure down. Buildings, walls, and by extension conventions.
Letting yourself down into a place and staying — a town, or a medical practice.
Slow, heavy descent. Literary: a body, a mist, a mood.
Pressure applied downward — a lever, or a person's spirits.
The formal version of hinsetzen. Placing down with deliberateness.

core: In front, in advance, presented forward
hint: Ahead in space or in time: placing before someone, or doing something beforehand.
feeling: vor- is in front of, and it splits neatly into space and time. In space, you hold something out in front of a person — which is how vorstellen (place before) becomes both 'introduce' and 'imagine', and how vorlesen becomes reading aloud to someone. In time, it is doing something beforehand: vorbereiten, vorhaben, vorsehen. There's a sharper third use where holding something in front of someone becomes accusation — vorwerfen, to throw it in their face. Notice how much of German's mental vocabulary lives here: to imagine is to set a thing before your own eyes.
mnemonic: Hold it out in front. Before someone's eyes (space) or before the event (time).

examples.why: Placing a person before others — or, reflexively, placing an image before your own mind.
Making ready ahead of time. The time branch in its plainest form.
Striking an idea forward into the room so the others can see it.
Reading out in front of a listener. What you do to a child at bedtime.
Pulling one option to the front of the queue. Preference as physical ranking.
Having something in front of you on the agenda. Was hast du vor?
Throwing the fault down in front of someone. Dative for the person accused.
Coming forward into view — an event happens, or something appears a certain way to you.
Seeing ahead and making arrangements. Vorsicht — caution — is the same root.
Going ahead. Was geht hier vor? = what's going on here?

core: Away, gone — removal in everyday speech
hint: The spoken, everyday 'away'. Blunter and more common than fort-.
feeling: weg- is the workhorse 'away'. Where ab- detaches something from a specific surface or starting point, weg- just removes it from the scene: it's gone, and where it went doesn't matter. That indifference is the feeling — wegwerfen is to throw away without a destination, weggehen is to leave without saying where. It's the most colloquial of the departure prefixes, and it stacks easily onto almost any action verb, which makes it a good one to experiment with: if you can think of an action, weg- plus that action almost certainly means doing it so the thing disappears.
mnemonic: 'Gone, and I don't care where.' ab- = off this; weg- = away from here.

examples.why: Leaving the scene. No destination implied — that's the difference from hingehen.
Taking something so it's no longer there. Often with a note of unfairness.
Throwing with disposal as the point. Wegwerfgesellschaft = throwaway society.
Fleeing the scene. Blunter and more everyday than entlaufen.
Departing by vehicle, or going away on a trip.
Letting a part be absent — the ingredient or the sentence isn't there.
Clearing things off the visible surface. What you do before guests arrive.
Dispatching a person or thing out of your space. Often a rejection.
Carrying something off — rubbish, a car to the garage, a child to school.
Turning your gaze away. Figurative too: ignoring what you should confront.

core: Onward, further, keep going
hint: The action continues past where it might have stopped, or passes to the next person.
feeling: weiter- comes from weit (far) and means further along. It is one of the most productive prefixes in modern German: attach it to almost any verb and you get 'carry on doing that'. Machen → weitermachen, carry on. That alone makes it worth learning early — it turns verbs you already know into new ones with zero risk. Its second use is passing onward: weiterleiten (forward an email), weitererzählen (pass a story on). Same line, but now the thing travels from you to the next person rather than continuing under your own steam.
mnemonic: 'And further.' Safest prefix to invent with — weiter- + almost any verb works.

examples.why: The template case. Doing what you were doing, further along the line.
Walking further — or a situation continuing. Es geht weiter = it continues.
Resuming the journey after a stop.
Directing something onward to the next recipient. The email verb.
Telling it further along the chain. Often with a warning: nicht weitererzählen!
Taking an existing thing and pushing its development onward.
Helping someone get past the point where they were stuck. Dative.
Educating yourself onward. Weiterbildung is standard on any German CV.
Work continuing past a break or a deadline.
Machines, contracts and costs that carry on whether you're watching or not.

core: Shut — and, oppositely, toward someone
hint: Two senses: closing something, or directing an action at a person. The dative is the clue.
feeling: zu- looks contradictory until you separate its two jobs. (1) Closing: zumachen, zuschließen — the gap is sealed. (2) Toward a person, from the preposition zu: zuhören is to direct your hearing at someone, zustimmen is to place your agreement with them. The two rarely get confused in practice because sense (2) almost always comes with a dative object — ich höre dir zu. A third, minor branch is addition: zunehmen, zugeben, something is added to a total. Watch for that dative and the ambiguity dissolves.
mnemonic: Dative present → 'toward that person'. No dative → 'shut'. Mach die Tür zu vs. hör mir zu.

examples.why: The closing sense at its simplest. Opposite of aufmachen.
Closing so it's sealed and secured. The extra zu- adds finality to schließen.
Hearing directed at a person. Hören is passive; zu- makes it deliberate. Dative.
Looking directed at something happening. Often with a hint of not intervening.
Placing your voice alongside theirs. Dative: ich stimme dir zu.
Giving something toward the truth — or adding an ingredient to the pot.
The addition branch: the total takes something on. Opposite of abnehmen.
Letting something come toward you rather than blocking it. Also: to license.
Ordering one thing toward another so they belong together. Dative.

examples.english: to approach; to be due to sb
examples.why: Something moving toward you. Auf mich zukommen — heading my way.

core: Back — return and reversal
hint: The action is undone or retraced. Maps almost perfectly onto English re-/back.
feeling: zurück- is back, and it is one of the most transparent prefixes for an English speaker: whatever the verb does, zurück- makes it go the other way or return to the origin. Geben → zurückgeben, give back. Rufen → zurückrufen, call back. There's no hidden second branch and no figurative trap, which makes it, like zer-, a good confidence-builder. The only nuance worth noting is restraint: zurückhalten, sich zurückziehen — pulling yourself back from involvement. Backwards motion becomes reticence.
mnemonic: English back or re- → German zurück-. One of the few near-perfect one-to-one mappings.

examples.why: Coming back to where you were. The core image with nothing added.
Reversing the direction of a gift or a loan.
Retracing your steps — or, of numbers, falling back to a lower level.
Returning a phone call. The call goes back the way it came.
Pulling yourself back out of a situation. The restraint branch.

examples.english: to put back; to cover a distance
examples.why: Putting a thing back on the shelf — or laying a stretch of road behind you.
Holding something so it doesn't go forward. Also zurückhaltend = reserved.
The more formal 'return'. Used of journeys, eras, and symptoms.
Sending the money back along the path it came. Loans and favours alike.
Pointing someone back the way they came. Refusal as reversed direction.

core: Together — joining, or collapsing into one
hint: Separate parts become a single thing. Sometimes constructively, sometimes catastrophically.
feeling: zusammen- means together, and it differs from mit- in an important way: mit- is about a person joining an action, while zusammen- is about parts merging into one whole. That merging can be productive (zusammenarbeiten, zusammenfassen) or destructive (zusammenbrechen, zusammenstoßen) — because a building collapsing is also, physically, its parts coming together. Keep that double edge in mind: zusammen- tells you things converge, not whether that's good news. It's a long prefix and it always carries the stress.
mnemonic: Two hands closing into one fist. Constructive merging or collapse — the prefix doesn't judge.

examples.why: Separate efforts merged into one piece of work.
Grasping scattered points and holding them as one. Zusammenfassung = summary.
Breaking such that the whole falls in on itself. Buildings, systems, people.
People converging on one place. Also: circumstances coinciding.
Placing separate items into a single arrangement — a playlist, a team, a menu.
Two things whose shapes agree. Used of colours, schedules, and couples.
Laying two things into one — departments, or a map folded flat.
Counting separate figures into one sum.
A group holding as one under pressure. Loyalty as physical cohesion.
The destructive edge: two things arriving at the same point at speed.

core: Toward and facing — meeting, or opposing
hint: Head-on. You move toward something that is moving toward you — to greet it or to resist it.
feeling: entgegen- is the head-on gesture: two things facing each other. That single image gives two opposite tones. Welcoming: entgegenkommen is to come to meet someone — and figuratively to accommodate them, to meet them halfway. Resisting: entgegenwirken, entgegenstehen, entgegentreten — facing something in order to block it. The prefix itself is neutral; the verb decides whether the meeting is a handshake or a stand-off. It's formal in register and almost always takes the dative, since you are facing toward something.
mnemonic: Two arrows pointing at each other. Greeting or confrontation — same geometry. Always dative.

examples.english: to come to meet; to accommodate
examples.why: Walking toward someone approaching you. Figuratively: meeting them halfway on terms.

examples.english: to look forward to; to face
examples.why: Looking at what's coming toward you — with anticipation or with resolve.
Taking something being handed toward you. Formal: prizes, deliveries, applications.
Carrying a feeling toward someone: Vertrauen entgegenbringen — to extend trust.

examples.english: to stand in the way of
examples.why: Standing facing the thing so it can't pass. The obstacle sense.
Acting in the opposing direction to reduce an effect. Policy and medicine both use it.
Stepping into the path of something. Used of prejudice, rumour, aggression.
Placing your position opposite theirs. Widerstand entgegensetzen — to put up resistance.
Holding an argument up in front of the other person's claim.

examples.english: to run toward; to run counter to
examples.why: Literally running to meet someone — or, figuratively, contradicting a principle.

core: Through — physically across, or thoroughly to the end
hint: Separable when a body passes through space. Inseparable when the action saturates something.
feeling: durch- is passage through a body or a barrier. The split follows a clean rule: when something literally travels through and out the other side, it is separable and stressed (Ich gehe durch). When the meaning becomes thoroughness — doing the action across the whole of something — it goes inseparable (durchsuchen, to search a place thoroughly). That second sense is where the real feeling lives: durch- verbs are exhaustive. You didn't read the book, you read it through. You didn't think about it, you thought it all the way through to the far side.
mnemonic: Literal passage → separable (ich gehe durch). Thoroughness → inseparable (ich durchsuche).

examples.english: to walk through; to go over sth
examples.why: Separable. Passing through a space — or going through a list item by item.
Separable. Reading from one end to the other, not sampling.
Separable. You fall through the net instead of being caught by it.
Separable. Holding on all the way through to the other side of a hard stretch.
Separable. Getting your position through the resistance. Reflexively: to prevail.
Thinking that traverses the whole problem rather than touching one corner.
Inseparable. Searching that covers every part — a house, a bag, a database.
Inseparable. Moving across the full width of a country, desert, or room.
Inseparable here. Your gaze passes through the pretence to the truth behind it.
Both, with different meanings: separable = snap in two; inseparable = break through a barrier.

core: Behind — left behind, or done behind someone's back
hint: A small, almost entirely inseparable set. Where German keeps its verbs of deceit.
feeling: hinter- is the space behind, and as a prefix it is nearly always inseparable and slightly sinister. Two branches. Leaving behind: hinterlassen, what remains after you. Behind someone's back: hintergehen (to deceive), hinterziehen (to evade tax), hinterbringen (to report secretly). German locates dishonesty spatially — it happens where you can't see. It's a closed, low-frequency set, so the honest list below includes the everyday nouns that share the feeling, since they are what you'll actually meet in print.
mnemonic: If it's behind your back, it's shady. hinter- is the prefix of things done out of sight.

examples.why: What remains after you've gone — a message, a mess, an inheritance.

examples.english: to deceive, go behind sb's back
examples.why: Moving around behind the person so they can't see what you're doing.
Asking what sits behind the surface claim. A favourite of German commentary.
Placing something behind the counter for safekeeping — money, a key, a deposit.
Pulling money out of sight behind the state's back. Steuerhinterziehung.
Driving a plan off course from behind, where the effort can't be traced.
Carrying information to someone behind the subject's back.
Holding position behind cover until the moment to strike. Same instinct, as a noun.
The ground behind the subject — of a picture, or of a story.
The exit nobody sees you use. Also a legal or contractual escape route.

core: Over — across, above, beyond the limit, or missed entirely
hint: Separable when something physically crosses or spills. Inseparable when it covers, exceeds, or overlooks.
feeling: über- is one of the richest prefixes. Separable and stressed, it is literal: something goes over an edge (überlaufen — to boil over, überkochen). Inseparable and unstressed, it fans out into four figurative senses. Across: überqueren, übersetzen (carrying meaning across languages). Beyond the limit: übertreiben, überleben — going past where you'd expect to stop. Covering: überzeugen, überdecken. And, most usefully, missing by passing over: übersehen is to look right over something and not see it. Same as English 'overlook', with exactly the same double edge.
mnemonic: Stress it and it's physical. Swallow the stress and it's figurative: beyond, across, or missed.

examples.why: Inseparable = translate (carry meaning across). Separable = physically ferry someone over.
Inseparable. Moving over a road, river or border to the far side.
Inseparable. Laying thoughts over a matter. Ich überlege es mir.
Your gaze passes over the thing without landing. The 'missing' branch.
Living beyond the event that should have ended it. The 'beyond' branch.
Driving the thing past its proper limit. Literally over-driving it.
Covering someone with evidence until their doubt is entirely overlaid.
Directing funds across from one account to another. The banking verb.
Taking a thing across from someone else's hands into yours — a role, a firm, a cost.
Separable = boil over the rim. Inseparable = to run over to the other side.

core: Around — encircling, turning, and therefore changing
hint: Separable when something turns or is redone differently. Inseparable when it surrounds.
feeling: um- means around, and the split is unusually satisfying. Inseparable = encircling, going around the outside: umarmen (put your arms around), umgeben (surround), umfahren (drive around an obstacle). Separable = turning around, hence changing: umziehen (change home or clothes), umsteigen (change trains), umdrehen (turn round). That second branch is the one to internalise — in German, to change something is to turn it around, which is why so many 'switch/convert/re-do' verbs start with um-. Beware the pair úmfahren (run over) vs. umfáhren (drive around) — stress alone is life or death.
mnemonic: Stressed úm- = turn it round, change it. Unstressed um- = go round the outside of it.

examples.english: to move house; to change clothes
examples.why: Separable. Both are turning yourself into a different arrangement — new flat, new outfit.
Separable. Climbing out and into a different one. Turning your journey around.
Separable, and the literal source of the whole 'change' branch.
Separable. Turning one item around into another. What you do with a bad gift.
Separable. Building the thing into a different shape. Also Umbau — renovation.
Separable. Turning fully around and retracing. Physical or moral.
Separable. Bleak logic: bringing someone around, out of life. Learn as a fixed item.
Inseparable. Your arms go around the person. The clearest encircling case.
Inseparable. Placed all around something. Umgebung = surroundings, area.

examples.english: to drive around / to run over
examples.why: The famous trap. Inseparable umfáhren = drive around it. Separable úmfahren = flatten it.

core: Under — beneath, supporting from below, or cutting off
hint: Separable when something physically goes under. Inseparable for subordination, interruption, and examination.
feeling: unter- starts beneath. Separable and stressed, it is literal descent (untergehen — to sink, to set). Inseparable, it branches three ways. Support from below: unterstützen — to prop up; unterhalten — to hold up, which becomes 'entertain' and 'maintain'. Getting underneath to examine: untersuchen, to investigate — searching beneath the surface. Cutting in from below: unterbrechen, to interrupt — breaking into something from underneath. And of course the plain hierarchical sense: unterdrücken, to press down and hold under.
mnemonic: Ask which way the force goes: propping up from below, or pressing down from above.

examples.why: Inseparable. Writing underneath the text — literally what a signature is.
Breaking into a flow from below and cutting it. Conversations, power supplies, journeys.
Searching beneath the surface for what isn't visible. Medical and criminal alike.
Stützen is to prop. Holding something up from underneath so it doesn't fall.
Holding up from below — a conversation, a guest's mood, or a household.
Pressing down so it stays under. People, feelings, and revolts.
Separating things by getting underneath what makes them different.
Taking a thing on and under your own responsibility. Unternehmen = enterprise.
Letting the action stay under — never letting it surface. Legal register.
Separable. The sun and the ship do the same thing: go under. Also: a culture collapsing.

core: Against — resistance and reflection
hint: Counter-force. Note the single 'e': wider = against. Not to be confused with wieder = again.
feeling: wider- means against, and it is the prefix of pushing back. Almost always inseparable, it forms verbs of contradiction and resistance: widersprechen, widerstehen, widerlegen. Its quieter second branch is reflection — a thing bouncing back off a surface: widerspiegeln (to mirror), widerhallen (to echo). Both are the same physics: something meets a surface and returns. Most wider- verbs take the dative for what is being resisted. Keep it apart from wieder- by spelling: one e means against, two mean again.
mnemonic: wider (one e) = against. wieder (two e's) = again. English with-stand keeps the old sense.

examples.why: Speaking against what was said. Dative: ich widerspreche dir.
Standing against a force. Temptation, pressure, an army. Dative.
Laying counter-evidence against a claim until it no longer stands.
Calling back against your own earlier statement. Legal and contractual.
Setting yourself against an order or authority. Dative.
An inner striving against the thing. Es widerstrebt mir — I find it distasteful.
Something travelling against you, arriving unbidden. Formal and often solemn.
The reflection branch. Separable. The image bounces back off the surface.
Sound returning from a wall. Same physics as the mirror.
The noun of speaking against. Also Widerstand — resistance.

core: Again, back — repetition and restoration
hint: Two e's: this is 'again'. Mostly separable; wiederholen is the notable exception.
feeling: wieder- means again, and it maps almost exactly onto English re-. Attach it to a verb and the action happens a second time, or the previous state is restored: wiederaufbauen (rebuild), wiederherstellen (restore), wiedersehen (see again — hence auf Wiedersehen, 'until we see each other again'). It is nearly always separable and stressed. The one exception you must memorise is wiederholen — inseparable, meaning 'to repeat'. Said separably, wieder holen, it means to fetch something again. Alongside weiter-, this is one of the safest prefixes to build new verbs with.
mnemonic: German wieder- ≈ English re-. Exception: wiederhólen (repeat) is inseparable.

examples.why: Meeting again after time apart. Auf Wiedersehen is this verb as a farewell.
Inseparable exception. Fetching the same thing back a second time — hence repeating it.
Coming a second time. Warmer and less formal than zurückkehren.
Giving the thing back out again — a quote, a performance, a colour on screen.
Finding what was lost. Also sich wiederfinden — to find yourself somewhere again.
Producing the original state again. The IT and medical restoration verb.
Recognition as knowing again — the arrival of er-, repeated.
Building up again after destruction. Wiederaufbau — postwar reconstruction.
Bringing life again. Used of patients, traditions, and neighbourhoods.
Uniting again what was split. Wiedervereinigung — German reunification, 1990.
